blocks.x: Let's see. This is the real one of Harold Dajon. What's the date, huh? The date is March the 29th, 1963. Yeah, and we're in room 101 of the history building.
And put your name on here, huh? Yeah, Kid Sheet.
What's your right name?
George Kohler.
Yeah, and I'm Dick Allen, but I'm going to let Sheet do the interviewing because Barry Martin wants this. All right. Just pick up the questions and just talk. Just go ahead and do it now.
Well, Harold, a little information on the bands, different bands. What brass band do you remember when you was a boy?

Well, I remember El Celsa, the Imperial, which is one of my favorite bands, the Imperial, Emmanuel Perez. I remember Allen's band from Over the River. I remember the Tuxedo Band. Celestat had a brass band called Tuxedo Brass Band. And I also remember Professor Ch된, he always kept a brass band with the fellas that he taught. Remember the Pacific band? And I remember the Holy Ghost Brass Band. I remember the Hanna-Pacific Brass Band a couple of times. Willie Parker. Yeah, Willie Parker. Yeah. And well, you know, I used to like to follow the Imperial Surinities, because I used to like to listen at, I thought about the example I played at alto. Yeah, he was playing. And Eddie Sheri used to play, he played playing at some time, and sometimes he played tenor.
It was probably Joe Wacken, who he was with. I don't remember what band he was with.
He played with Manny Parise. He was with one of them bands. No, Parise, but that was the Ormond band. Yeah. That's why he was the Imperial Surinities.
Well how does and what they played compared with the New Orleans brass bands of today?

Well, I'll tell you, the numbers they played the day most every brass band hit the street, you know, except the Eureka, the Young Tuxedo, bands like that. Well I would say the Dejan's Olympia brass band might bring some music out, you know. The Eureka always brings the music out, and a long time ago, the bands, very few brass bands didn't use music, most all of them had music. But they used to cut the name off the music, so when they hired a fellow to play at the band, he don't know what number he's playing, make sure he's reading his part. He used to, you take and cut the number off the top of the music and give it to you, it'd be a number, like sudden such a number. Sands. Yeah, get in the pack, say, let's play sudden such a number.
Same way to do the day.

Yeah, they do the same thing today, but some of the bands today, every time they hit the street, they're just a close to a walk of a day. Every time they hit the street. So that's why every night in the street, if they don't actually just a close to a walk, they have to play everything else but just a close to a walk with me.
Well, when do you remember saxophone being introduced in the brass band?

Well, no, no, no, it's like I tell you, when Manner Perez was a brass band, that's the first time that I heard the saxophone with the brass band, because he always used a saxophone. Yeah, I thought Alexander was playing alto, and like I told you before, Eddie Sherry was playing E-flat clatter, sometimes he'd play tenor instead. Well that would say back in the twenties when they had the saxophone. Oh yeah, in the twenties, yeah, beginning of the twenties, low-hilly twenties. Well, yeah, I would say, I'd say in the Brown in 1919, 1920 like that, yeah, that's what I remembered.
Well, how does the brass band play that's different from jazz playing?

Well, most of the brass bands, they play a watching tempo to walk, and like people are, when you're playing a brass band, you play maybe a six-eighth or two-fourth tempo, like some people call it split time, but it's two-fourth or six-eighth. Four-fourth, too. Yeah, they call it four-fourth, but they play it in two-fourth time. If they play a number, four-fourth number, they're going to play it in two-fourth time, but instead of saying two-fourth, they call it split time. That's what they call it, but it end up being two-fourth right on. The only number they play in four-fourth time is the funeral marches. And I was looking at a few marches the other day, I can't think, I can't remember the name of it right now, but it was in three-fourth time. I can't think of the name of it, by Professor Pritchard Howard.
Has Perrier the music changed in your auction during the last thirty years?

Yeah, yeah, yes, it did a little, because they had better bass drum players years ago. It looked like the bass drum players was different. In fact, they had more of them, and more brass bands. That's the biggest reason for them to chant that, like Inez Rapana and Lil Jim and then the Black Van and them were rough bass drum players, you know. Because you've got some good bass drum players now, but I mean you can count them out on one hand. Count them out on one hand. See, because you've got to play a few marches, you play it from your heart and soul, some of them just be beating, counting full. You know, one, two, three, four, like the funeral marches go.
But in other words, I mean the parade music hadn't changed any.

It hadn't changed, the style hadn't changed, no, the style hadn't changed. Just like I said, before they just had more bands, they may have had more musicians, and they had a lot better musicians, because the top-notches most, that played these funerals and stuff, the majority of the top-notches have passed away. Of course they still have some here, you know, a few, but the top-notch parade, man, most of them is gone.
Did the old brass bands use a lot more sheet music than today?

Yes, they did. They did. Because you see, and before, when you're playing the brass band, you have to rehearse them. See when I was playing the Holy Ghost brass band, my dad had a voice about my youth plant clarinet. I was a youngster, in my teens. But we had to rehearse them at the Holy Ghost Hall twice a week. And Landry was a first drummer with the band, and Pinchback Two-Rows directing the band. So we used to rehearse them twice a week, because they had to rehearse on that music, and if you didn't show up to rehearse them, it would get somebody in your place, because when they hit the street, you know, they wanted to hit it right.
And then I guess at that time it was, most of the fellas was mostly sheet men, I mean,
read them. Yeah, most of them. They were better than they were in my head. That's what mostly kept me in the band at that time, you know, because I could read them parts.
Are they playing the same numbers now as they did them?

Yeah, they played a lot of the same, some of the same numbers, but you don't hear all the numbers like you used to hear a long time ago, because the fellas, the brass band, just hit the street, they'd play shake it and break it all the way through, just like supposed to be, they'd play Panama Rag all the way down. The bands now, they'd say Panama Rag, they might start writing the chorus or something. Now you catch a band like Eureka, and if they're playing Panama Rag, they'll play it all the way. Sometime and sometimes they don't. Go the short route. Yeah, they go the short route. They call that the short route.
There are not Perez bands in the Orleans played in six eighth time or any other time than four fourths?

Well, I told you before they played six eighth and two fourth time and they have four fourth mark on the music, but if you're going to play a march, you can't play a march on a four fourth tempo, you'll be playing it two fourth time or split time.
Who are some of the best old bands?

What do you mean the old parade band? Yeah. The El Seltzer, the Hornward, the band band that the parade was leading, and the Tuxedo, you know, one Celestad. Imperial. Well yeah, Imperial, and Old Man Allen had a good band too. When you played in the Old Man Allen band you had to clean your eyes out, because he always put that music in front of you. He used to go play all that with him. That's right. He would put that music in front of you all the time. I played with him once in my life.
You didn't know if he could read or not he could read.
He didn't know if he could read. I played with him with Old Man Allen's band once.
What brass band did you play with before you organized a Dijon on MP brass band?

Well, I played with Eureka quite some time, and when I went to work in the day, I couldn't make the funeral through the week, so eventually he got somebody that could play the funeral through and then I joined the Chasm, the Young Tuxedo brass band. Yeah. Yeah. But I always kept a band on my own, because sometimes a band would get two jobs and I would take my band out.
Who was Lil Jim? Lil Jim was a bass drum player.
He had a bass drum, you couldn't see him in the back of him. The bass drum was bigger than him. You could hardly see him in the back of him.
And they had other names they called?

I don't remember his other names. Yeah, they called him the Hog. Yeah, but I never did remember these other names. When was your band? 4th of February of 1909. New Orleans? New Orleans, yes, New Orleans. Good old days.
Good old days.

Yeah, good old days. I started taking lessons on him, about eight or nine years old or something like that. Who was your teacher? Well, first I went to Professor Nickerson because Lorenzo Teal was in New York. And my brother was supposed to go to Mary Perez, and Mary Perez in New York, so he went to Charleneene. And I went to Professor Nickerson. So when Lorenzo Teal came back from New York, well, I went to Lorenzo Teal. In other words, that's my teacher, Lorenzo Teal, because that's where I really learned how to read and play. Professor Nickerson was a wonderful teacher, but he was a violinist, you know. He could teach all instruments. It's not like going, like if you're going to a fellow that played an instrument that you want to learn, it's better.
Brass band jobs after the Holy Ghost. Poise brass band jobs after the Holy Ghost.

After I left the Holy Ghost brass band, can I remember Poise brass band, John? Let's see, I think it must have been with Charleneene, because we played the cornerstone laying with Charleneene's brass band, with the St. John the Bois, right across the street from Dillard, we laid the cornerstone with Charleneene's brass band. I don't remember the year right now, but it's been a long time.
Do you remember the last year when you played?
The last year when I played was about two months ago, I think.
I played less than that.
About a month or two ago.
Oh, that was with your band then? Yeah, with the Olympia brass band.

You see I used to play with Eureka when I had a band I scored the number two Eureka. And when I fixed them to make this recording they decided that I should chant my name. And I told them I played with the Arnoldi Pass, Olympia Syrenet, it was a long time. And I don't think they ever had a band they called Olympia brass band, so I thought I would name my band an Olympia brass band.
Did you name the favorites in the brass band?

Well, they're always my favorite, but in the brass band I had Sheik and Orny Canyon Leonard. Sometimes used three trumpets, sometimes used two trumpets and three reeds and Jesse Charles. And used Clarence and I used Louis Couture or Willie Humphrey.
Tramon?
Tramon and Nelson. Tramon.

Nelson and Eddie Summers. I mean them your favorite fellas. Yeah. In the old days. In the old days. What favorite music that I liked the best? Well in the street my favorite trumpet player was Manuel Perez and Red Allen in the street. That's my favorite trumpet player. Manuel Perez, Red Allen, Willie Pazio and so he's living in Nightward, Maurice Duran. And then later on when Guy Kelly came here, I used to like to hear Guy play too because he could blow. He was very powerful in the street you see. And a powerful man in the street he was always noticing. I used to really like to hear him play. I mean not leaving Mr. Landry because he was a very good street man too. And Shotzi was a very good street man. But my favorite like I said, Man of the Reyes, Willie Pazio, Pushy Humphrey, Ray Allen, Guy Kelly. You know that. Yeah. It was good. And another one, you see I used to, so many good trumpet players you used to admire them all. Not all but I mean you used to admire them like Wooden Joe. He was a good street man too. Yeah. Yeah. And your prime ones and the sacks players. In your old days. Well in the old days, well, Lorenzo Teo and Willie Humphrey was my favorite clarinet players. Was my favorite. Well after them, I kept the following me of Eddie Sherif. If he's playing his
he fled a car that day. Well you didn't know too much about Joe Watkins and he was pretty a famous client. Yeah. Well I didn't know too much about him. I

know a lot about George Boyd and Zeb because I used to play with George Boyd at the Willow Inn. Me, George Boyd, Udell, Willie Dennis Boyd, and when George Boyd couldn't come he used to send John Casper. Well back in that time John was. John John started to play clarinet jack. He was playing for his flat clarinet. George Boyd just had to you know beg him sometimes to go at his place because I mean he didn't think he'd be playing behind George Boyd but he used to play
all right. And the alto horns and your baritone horns, tubas you know.

I'll get back in the background. Big Eddie Jackson on that Sousa horn. That was my favorite Sousa horn player. Big Eddie Jackson, Old Man Kimball too. Old Man Kimball played nice Sousa horn too. Eddie Jackson, Old Man Kimball, and I remember another good Sousa horn player. His name used to live on Simon Bob. Correct. No. Page. No. No, very not. He'd play clarinet, that's when I was playing Riddles Tuxedo. John Porter. John Porter. John Porter. And this other fella played good Sousa horn too which was a tremor like that. His mouth was a tremor when he'd go to Sousa horn. He used to be a trumpet player. One time he used to play trumpet. Joe Howard. Joe Howard. He was a good Sousa horn player. Good Sousa horn player. And Old Man Kimball, he used to play Sousa horn too and then he played Sousa horn in the orchestra with us when I was on the road
of the desert. And this fella, he used to play at the Ricca Band until he died, Ferret. Ferret. You remember that? Ferret, yeah. He used to wear the apron. Yeah. He was pretty good. Yeah.

And your snare drummers. Well, one of the snare drummers, I used to like Alfred. You're talking back in the old and old. Well, yeah, I used to like Alfred and I was stuff I don't remember if he was a good snare drum player. And this fellow used to play a snare drum with the Eureka Brass Band a long time ago. Well, there were two good drummers there, a good snare drum player, Evo Wells used to play with the Golden Ghost Brass Band, he was a good snare drum player as well. You said Alfred, who he was? Alfred Williams.
And you said Happy.
Yeah, Happy Goldstein. Oh, I see. I see. And I call this what you spell on the roof garden, Manuel Perez. He used to play in the Brass Band sometimes, and he'd play a drum all day.
Not Faiso.
When Humphrey was playing trombone with the band, well Humphrey was playing trombone with the band.
I see. It wasn't Faiso.

No, I don't remember anything. Now, but the best snare drum player in all of them in the street was old man Cottrell. Man, that's who he used to play with, Manuel Perez. That's where I saw him, old man Cottrell, old man Lutz Cottrell. 된 stuff with
In the Perez, I wouldn't say as far back as where the men and then, but I mean they still had fellas playing, you know, running times. Or anything you'd say like Howard, he was playing.

Well Howard was an ace, man. Howard was powerful, just like Kid René and Albert Snyad. And I'd say my brother Leo, he's a very powerful trumpet player, a good first-chair man, but Howard was a good street man. Don't care what you play, he would play it. Very powerful.
And Leo, he wasn't much of a street man.

Leo was a good street man at the time because the brass band he played with had the music, you see, and he could read anything they put up there. And that's why Shawnee Neen was crazy about him. But he didn't play too much brass band work. Mostly he played like with Shawnee Neen, you know, and brass bands like that. He did most of the orchestra work, played with Pierron, you know, and had the band they made up around there, the band there. And he played with Rizzly Tuxedo when I was playing with him. And he played with Lyrus a long time. And they had the Sonny South, a band that they made up. Who was Leo? Leo Daniel, that was my brother. The first band we had together was the Moonlight Serenade. We were on trumpet man. I was playing clarinet and alto saxophone. We had two altos in saxophone man. Henry Cavanaugh and Alto, where I know him played drums, called him Bazoo for a nickname. And I had Reuben McClendon. There's no Sidney Cage was playing banjo at the time. Sidney Cage was playing banjo. Sidney Cage was the manager of the band and he was the leader of the band. And Albert Fernandez was playing trumpet at the time too, and he's still playing trumpet.
Well, what trumpet player plays Sid now, much which or not?
Well, my main trumpet player now is Kid Sheik. That's my main trumpet player. You all get around and play it all?
Oh, yeah, we get around and play it all.

We play most of the job. We play with one another. If he can get a job, I got it. If I get a job, he's got it. And then I still play extra with the record when I need an extra man, well, I'm still playing with him right on. My band gets a job, he's going to play any job I get. So I have to say right now, that's about my favorite trumpet player right now.
Well, I think we're about to run out a little bit now.

Well, let's not leave George McCollum out, Alvin Alcorn. See, as you talk, you think, you see? Think like George McCollum. George McCollum was a, he ain't number one trumpet man, but he was better when you put the music up there too. He was great. I remember one time in Basin, Mississippi, we was playing with Desdun, we was playing the advertisement. George McCollum picked up a number, nobody knew what number and what it was, but it sounds some good. And everybody fell right on in there with him, and the people started dancing in the street and everything. So we was playing in front of this drugstore where every time we go to Basin, we go play in front of this drugstore, the man gives all the seagull. So they asked George, what the devil did you pick up there? Yeah. I said, man, that sounds some good. We never heard of Davenport, George. I said, that's a seagull stomp. Yeah, you just pick up a number. You know, you went to pick up one number and pick up another number. That number ever could have been recorded. I think it would have been, went over big. Yeah, yeah. Yeah, well I think, but covered, but I could talk, I guess a couple hours on good trumpet players, and things, we've got a lot of them around here. We had a lot of them done, still got a lot of them around here. Thomas Jefferson, Joe Phillip, all those good trumpet players. He's playing good again. Howard was sick, but he's getting back like kid Howard one more time. He's living a second life now. If you'd have seen the way he looked when I went to the hospital, you would know what I mean when I say he's living a second life. He lived two lives. He lived one and he's living a second one right now. I don't know. Yeah. Well, in a brass band, I've been using Josiah Freddie, they call him Saeed on snare drum, Henry Glass on bass drum, and when Saeed can't play, well Paul Byrath always take his place. Sometimes the band might use three reeds, cryin' that and two saxons, sometimes one saxon, one cryin' that and three trumpets. They usually carry ten pieces, but every nine in the brass band tries to stick another one in, which is eleven, and I think they ought to carry eleven or twelve pieces all the time, because it would sound a lot better. And another thing I want to mention, we've got a drum player around here, but the only one close to Black Benny's playing is Henry Glass. He's the closest bass drum player to Black Benny. In fact, I think that's where you guys inspiration from. And a long time ago when Black Benny was popular, you had to play it because they had so many good things. Of course they had a lot of good trombone players too in them days, like Sonny Henry, Louis Warner, and when I was playing Rita Tuck City he had a trombone player with him. I never could think of the man's name, but he played some trombone. Were the good readers ever very hot? Were they very hot?
I mean the readers?
Well, some of them. But you see, a good reader, in them days a good reader looked like when you took a hot chorus, it was a little different, hot, from a man that couldn't read.
In other words, they could get off?

Yeah, sure they could get off. Man Perez could get off pretty good, and he was a good reader. I know him at Twyler, get off a little bit, beautiful, he was a good trumpet player. George McCollum could get off. Leo, he could get off.
Do you remember when Bunk was playing brass bands?
Bunk Johnson, I remember Bunk Johnson, but I don't remember what brass band he was playing, I really don't remember. But I remember seeing him playing with different bands.
Who played on the street and in the dance bands? Who played in the street and not in the dance bands?

Well, there were a few of them played in the street and not in the dance bands, because some of them played in the street and then if a band gets in the jam or something like that, they'll hire them to play in a dance band, see? Like Sonny Henry, he was a better street man than he was a dance man, see? He did most parade work and funerals and stuff, but if you had to hire him to play in an auction, he made it all right. He played good.
Yeah, he played his band. Yeah.
He played Rene, but I mean he was a better street man.
Just like you take Warner.
Yeah, Warner too. Warner's a better street man, but now you'd be surprised. Warner get in the office and play some trombone. Yeah, Warner really play some trombone now.
And about Chicken Henry.
Well, Chicken Henry, yeah, he's all right. Chicken Henry's a pretty good trombone player. Old time. Yeah, good old time. Chicken Henry's a pretty good trombone player.
Did they have, did they have Tom Brass band?

Yes, indeed. When Allen and them hit the street, when Ray Allen and them hit the street, I mean, Ray Allen and Guy Kelly, when he was playing with his dance band, Walter Pichon was playing mellow for him with them. When they hit the street, probably didn't roll up. I'm telling you.
And them bands used to advertise on them trucks.

On the trucks, yeah. They'd like Chris Kelly, Kid Renee, Punch, another good trombone I used to have around here, too. The Albus and I had. But Chris Kelly, Punch, Renee, you'd see them maybe every Sunday. Every Sunday. Every Sunday you could maybe look for them on a truck or a furniture wagon. First, you'd go on a furniture wagon, pulled by a mule or a horse, then later on they'd start going on trucks.
Well, they'd meet up sometime on the corner?

Some of them meet up on the corner sometime, and it'd be just like a price fight. The best man wins. Sometimes they'd be fighting the street, arguing about who's got the best band. Yeah. But Lil' Turk always come through that cut, because he could blow. Yeah. And they'd play all them pieces like Panama, Shakin' and Break It, Avalon. He was really on the ball. And old Chris, he'd come through. Oh, Chris come through with that blues with that little shot, call that, and that plunger and play the blues.

segments.title: Interview opening and handing questions to Kid Sheik
segments.summary: Dick Allen states the date and place, identifies Kid Sheik (George Kohler), and lets Sheik do the interviewing.

segments.title: Brass bands remembered from boyhood
segments.summary: Dejan lists the brass bands he remembers (Imperial, Allen's, Tuxedo, Holy Ghost and others) and sidemen like Eddie Cherie.

segments.title: How today's brass bands compare; music with names cut off
segments.summary: Dejan compares old and current bands' repertoire, and describes cutting the titles off music so hired players call tunes by number.

segments.title: Saxophone enters the brass band
segments.summary: He first heard saxophone in Manuel Perez's brass band around 1919-20.

segments.title: Brass band tempo versus jazz, and how parade music has changed
segments.summary: Brass bands play split time (two-four or six-eight) with funeral marches in four-four; bass drummers were better and bands more numerous before, but the style is unchanged.

segments.title: Reading music and rehearsals in the Holy Ghost band
segments.summary: Old bands used sheet music and rehearsed twice a week; Dejan was kept in the band because he could read. Some current bands play tunes like Panama Rag the short way.

segments.title: Best old bands, Old Man Allen, and Dejan's own brass band career
segments.summary: He names the best old bands, recalls playing once with Old Man Allen, then Eureka and the Young Tuxedo, while always keeping his own band.

segments.title: Lil Jim the bass drummer and Dejan's birth date
segments.summary: Lil Jim's huge bass drum; Dejan gives his birth as February 4, 1909.

segments.title: Lessons with Nickerson and Lorenzo Tio
segments.summary: He began lessons at eight or nine with Professor Nickerson, then Lorenzo Tio, from whom he really learned to read and play.

segments.title: Brass band jobs after Holy Ghost and naming the Olympia band
segments.summary: He recalls playing with Charleneene's band, his most recent job, and why he named his own band the Olympia Brass Band.

segments.title: Dejan's Olympia lineup and favorite street trumpet players
segments.summary: Current Olympia personnel, then his favorite street trumpeters (Manuel Perez, Red Allen, Guy Kelly, Wooden Joe) and clarinetists.

segments.title: Playing with George Boyd at the Willow Inn
segments.summary: He played with George Boyd at the Willow Inn, where John Casimir would sub on clarinet.

segments.title: Favorite tuba and snare drum players
segments.summary: Big Eddie Jackson, Old Man Kimball, John Porter and Joe Howard on sousaphone; snare drummers Alfred Williams, Happy Goldston, and Old Man Cottrell.

segments.title: Kid Howard and Leo Dejan as street trumpeters
segments.summary: Howard was a powerful street man; Dejan's brother Leo read anything, did orchestra work, and played in their first band, the Moonlight Serenade.

segments.title: Kid Sheik as Dejan's main trumpeter
segments.summary: Kid Sheik and Dejan share work, each calling the other for jobs.

segments.title: George McCollum, Olympia personnel, trombonists and readers who could play hot
segments.summary: McCollum picking up an unknown tune in Bay St. Louis, Olympia instrumentation, Henry Glass as bass drummer, and whether good readers could swing.

segments.title: Street players versus dance band players, with a Bunk Johnson aside
segments.summary: Some trombonists were better parade men than dance men, though still capable in the dance hall.

segments.title: Bands advertising on trucks and competing on street corners
segments.summary: Bands advertised from furniture wagons and trucks, met on corners like a prize fight, with Chris Kelly, Punch and Kid Rena.
